sentences.text: This animal belongs to the genus Achelousaurus, with the specific species name horneri.
It is estimated to have been about 6 meters long and weighed approximately 3 metric tons.
The creature possessed a bony neck frill featuring a pair of long spikes that curved outward.
Adults had rough, roundish bosses located above the eyes and on the snout.
The genus is known from few specimens, mainly skull material ranging from juveniles to adults.
It had a large head with a hooked beak, large nasal openings, and dental batteries containing hundreds of stacked teeth.
There were between 25 and 28 tooth positions in each upper jaw bone.
Paleontologists proposed that the rugose bosses were covered by thick pads of keratinized skin, similar to the bosses of modern muskoxen.
Scott D. Sampson named the species Achelousaurus horneri after describing the genus in 1994.
The first fossils were collected in Montana in 1987.
Within Ceratopsia, Achelousaurus belongs to the clade Pachyrostra, or "thick-snouted" dinosaurs.
It lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 77 to 74.8 million years ago, specifically during the Campanian age and stage.
It inhabited the island continent of Laramidia within the Two Medicine Formation.
There is a debate regarding its evolutionary lineage; later discoveries suggest it is closely related to Pachyrhinosaurus within the group Pachyrhinosaurini.
Researchers hypothesize that the bosses were used for fighting by butting heads and for display.
Jack Horner initially focused less on horned dinosaurs than on hadrosaurs.
It is debated whether the subadult specimen MOR 591 belongs to Achelousaurus or Einiosaurus, with some researchers suggesting the latter in 2021.
